title: Obama Judge Torpedoes Trump's Birthright Do-Over: Even Terrorists' Kids Are Citizens
desc:
Obama Judge Torpedoes Trump's Birthright Do-Over: Even Terrorists' Kids Are Citizens

An Obama-appointed federal judge in Washington on Wednesday blocked President Trump's second attempt to narrow birthright citizenship, ruling that the government can't refuse to recognize as Americans the US-born children of members of designated terrorist groups, foreign government employees, or foreigners who pay a surrogate to give birth here.

US District Judge Christopher Cooper certified a class and issued a preliminary injunction barring the State Department, the Department of Homeland Security and the Social Security Administration from enforcing Trump's August executive order against the children covered by the suit, Nathan v. Trump, which the ACLU and allied groups filed in September.

"The merits in this case are clear-cut," Cooper wrote in a 67-page opinion. The Supreme Court, he wrote, "has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are U.S. citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to U.S. law."

And the President, he added, "cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws."

BREAKING: Obama-appointed District Judge Christopher Cooper just BLOCKED Trump's August Executive Order, which restricts birthright citizenship for the children of foreign government officials, terrorist groups, and accused fraudsters. pic.twitter.com/P9ZkDnxHFU

— Libs of TikTok (@libsoftiktok) November 25, 2026

Executive Order 14418, signed Aug. 6, tells federal agencies not to issue, or accept, documents recognizing US citizenship for a child when neither parent is a citizen and one of several conditions applies. Either parent is an "alien enemy," which the order defines to include any member of a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization or a Specially Designated Global Terrorist; either parent works for a foreign government, from ambassadors and embassy or consulate staff to employees of international organizations with immunity; or either parent "engaged in a commercial transaction to purchase or access birthright citizenship," including paying a surrogate in the US to give birth. It also reaches children born in US territories where federal law doesn't confer citizenship.

The White House billed the order as "consistent with historical exceptions to birthright citizenship recognized by the Supreme Court," according to its fact sheet, and Trump signed a companion order the same day, Ending Birth Tourism, directing the State Department and DHS to restrict visas for foreigners who come to give birth.

"This is just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by Obama," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said, adding that the order "is consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court."

The ACLU's Cody Wofsy, deputy director of its Immigrants' Rights Project, said Trump "needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land."

Cooper's ruling is the second injunction against the August order. In September, Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland blocked it for a class of children born after Feb. 19, 2025, finding it "almost certainly unconstitutional as applied to the certified class." To enforce the order, the administration now has to overturn both.

Cooper is the same judge who in May ordered Trump's name taken off the Kennedy Center, after which Trump went after the judge's wife, Arnold & Porter partner Amy Jeffress, as "a Radical Left Democrat." In June a conservative watchdog, the Center to Advance Security in America, filed a misconduct complaint arguing he should have stepped aside in that case because Jeffress, the group said, "currently represents Biden in ongoing litigation against President Trump."

The August order was Trump's answer to the Supreme Court's June 30 ruling in Trump v. Barbara, which struck down his first-day order denying citizenship to children of parents in the country illegally or temporarily. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote for the majority, leaning on the 1898 Wong Kim Ark precedent; Justice Brett Kavanaugh agreed on statutory grounds, and Justices Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch dissented.

Attorney General Todd Blanche has since said the Justice Department is going after birth tourism with existing fraud laws. "Those cases can be difficult to prove, but it's not slowing us down," he said in October.

Kavanaugh's view that the first order collided with federal statute rather than the Constitution handed Republicans their next play: Sen. Jim Banks' Citizenship Act, which would classify illegal entrants and birth tourists as "invaders" under federal law. Like any immigration bill, it would need 60 votes to get past a Senate filibuster.

title: Russian Ballistic Missile Attack On Ukrainian Capital Hits Shopping Center, Many Wounded
desc:
Russian Ballistic Missile Attack On Ukrainian Capital Hits Shopping Center, Many Wounded

There's been another largescale missile and drone attack on Ukraine overnight, following President Putin earlier in the week vowing that severe retaliation for Ukraine's long-range drone strikes on refineries was "inevitable".

The Ukrainian capital has continued to get the brunt of missile and drone attacks, and in this latest instance a shopping center was reportedly hit, wounding at least seven people.

The Kyiv City Military Administration cited that of these seven victims several were hospitalized, and with two in serious condition.

In addition to the attack on the shopping center, the city's mayor said an industrial building and a non-residential building in the city's Desnyanskyi district were hit.

The attack unfolded shortly before midnight, with Ukrainian media describing of total numbers overnight:

Russia launched an unspecified number of ballistic missiles, as well as 113 drones, 76 of them jet-powered, at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine's Air Force reported. As of 8 a.m. local time, air defenses shot down or suppressed 87 drones, 52 of them jet-powered, the Air Force said.

In all, authorities say that Russia targeted at least 20 locations, with drone debris falling over half-a-dozen others.

But there was also a deadly assault on Russian-controlled Zaporizhia in southeast Ukraine. A Russian-installed official there said that five people were killed and three more wounded in a Ukrainian drone attack.

"Following an enemy drone attack on a parking lot, five people were killed and three others wounded in the locality of Vesioloye," Governor Yevgeny Balitsky wrote on Telegram on Thursday.

Ukrainians are meanwhile bracing for ramped-up Russian aerial operations going into winter. Reuters this week wrote that "Preparations for potential Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian utility infrastructure this winter, particularly in regions near the border, are a top priority for ​the government, Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin said on Wednesday."

"Russia ‌has been striking Ukrainian civilian energy infrastructure since the start of the war, causing major disruptions, especially in large cities," the report added. These attacks have regularly sent residents in Ukrainian towns and cities scrambling for emergency shelter, oftentimes in underground metro stations.

title: Explosive Book Claims Bob Iger Got An ABC Underling Pregnant While He Was Her Boss
desc:
Explosive Book Claims Bob Iger Got An ABC Underling Pregnant While He Was Her Boss

Former Disney CEO Bob Iger had an extramarital affair in the early 1990s with an ABC marketer who reported to him while he ran ABC Entertainment, and she became pregnant, according to an unauthorized biography that hits shelves next week.

In The House of Mouse, Wall Street Journal reporter Robbie Whelan writes that the woman "suffered through a traumatic termination procedure." The New York Times, which obtained an advance copy, reported the allegation on Wednesday. The book describes the relationship as consensual, and the woman is not named.

JUST IN: Former Disney CEO Bob Iger accused of impregnating an ABC employee while serving as her boss.

FILE - Former Disney CEO Bob Iger arrives at the premiere of "Avengers: Endgame" in Los Angeles on April 22, 2019. (Photo by Jordan Strauss/Invision/AP, File)

— Polymarket (@Polymarket) November 26, 2026

Iger declined to be interviewed for the book. According to Whelan, a lawyer for Iger contacted him to raise concerns about "false and defamatory" claims. Disney, which declined to cooperate with the author, called Iger "one of the most respected CEOs of his generation."

According to the Times, Whelan ties the episode to Iger's public embrace of the #MeToo movement in the late 2010s.

The 528-page book, four years in the making, is out Dec. 1 from William Morrow, a HarperCollins imprint. Iger handed the top job to parks chief Josh D'Amaro in March, and stays on as a senior adviser and board member until his retirement on Dec. 31.

The book The House of Mouse (via hollywoodreporter.com)

In April, Puck reported that Disney had retained Charles Harder, the litigator who has represented Donald Trump, to push back on the book, and that Harder sent letters to HarperCollins about it.

Whelan portrays Iger as insecure, vindictive and preoccupied with money, and traces his drive to his father's suicide attempt when Iger was 12. He quotes a private 2014 email Iger sent to then-Marvel chairman Ike Perlmutter: "I am frustrated about compensation! I had a nasty and distasteful negotiation to extend my contract this last time."

In his new book "House of Mouse," WSJ reporter Robbie Whelan reveals how longtime Disney CEO Bob Iger and Marvel chairman Isaac "Ike" Perlmutter went from confidants to bitter enemies. 🔗 https://t.co/kgxksdVD0w pic.twitter.com/GXytYMBIav

Robbie Whelan (portrait) (via us.headtopics.com)

— The Wall Street Journal (@WSJ) November 25, 2026

Whelan writes that at a 2022 Marvel premiere, then-CEO Bob Chapek, Iger's successor and later rival, gestured at fans in costume and asked, "Did you get a look at the freaks?"

Iger's own next book, One Last Time, about his 2022 return to Disney, is due in March.

title: "Prepared For The Worst": UK Tells 100,000 Veterans To Be Ready For Call-Up
desc:
"Prepared For The Worst": UK Tells 100,000 Veterans To Be Ready For Call-Up

Britain's military chiefs have written to about 100,000 former service personnel in the Strategic Reserve, the first mass mailing of its kind since the Cold War, and Defense Secretary Wes Streeting says the public "should find it reassuring rather than alarming."

NEW - UK Defense Secretary says that "People should find it reassuring rather than alarming," that 100,000 strategic reservists have been sent a letter, for the first time since the cold war, to prepare to be called up for war. pic.twitter.com/ukACzhxD49

— Disclose.tv (@disclosetv) November 26, 2026

"So to some extent, what's happening today should be routine, but hasn't happened for some time," Streeting told Sky News on Thursday, confirming a report first carried by The Telegraph. "We have written out to our strategic reserve. These are people who previously served in our armed forces."

Wes Streeting refused to answer a question on Sky News (Image: Sky News)

The letters, signed by the heads of the Royal Navy, the British Army and the Royal Air Force, ask recipients to update their contact details and to say what skills they have picked up and what work they do now. They also invite the veterans to volunteer for training and exercises, including NATO's Steadfast Defender exercise next spring.

Streeting said it is information the government "ought to hold as standard, whatever the threat environment." Britain, he said, is "operating in a heightened threat environment. And so this degree of readiness, I think, is a sensible, necessary precaution."

He insisted Britain is "not imminently facing war," and reached for the pandemic to explain the timing. If the MoD didn't act now, he said, "it's the sort of thing that in a public inquiry in 20 or 30 years' time, people would be saying, why weren't the Ministry of Defense ready?" Those, he said, are "exactly the sort of findings we've seen coming out of the COVID inquiry," a lesson he took from his time as health secretary.

The Strategic Reserve is made up of former regulars who remain liable for recall in a "national danger, great emergency or attack on the UK." In January the Ministry of Defense announced that the Armed Forces Bill would raise the maximum recall age from 55 to 65 and allow former troops to be recalled for "warlike preparations" as well.

General view of the Ministry of Defence headquarters in Whitehall, London (Leon Neal / Getty Images)

The letters go out with the regular Army down to about 73,000 soldiers, its smallest since the Napoleonic Wars, and weeks after Streeting warned that Britain has "a little over 1,000 days" to be ready to fight and win alongside its allies, as the government told households to stock up on water, food and emergency supplies. The head of the British Army has gone further, telling Britons they must make sacrifices for a coming war.

"We do need to build our national resilience, build our readiness and make sure that we are prepared for the worst," Streeting said, "even as we're taking steps every day that make that worst case scenario less likely."

title: Futures Extend Thanksgiving Turnaround As Nasdaq Dodges Bear Market, Oil Climbs On Houthi Strikes
desc:
Futures Extend Thanksgiving Turnaround As Nasdaq Dodges Bear Market, Oil Climbs On Houthi Strikes

US futures are higher on Thanksgiving morning as Wednesday's violent intraday reversal, which saw the Nasdaq 100 dip into a bear market before closing down just 0.6%, carries over into a broad global risk rebound, with the AI trade getting a second wind even as S&P put Nvidia on negative credit watch, Nvidia froze server shipments to four Southeast Asian nations and lenders slammed the brakes on Chinese data center loans; oil meanwhile is higher again after Yemen's Houthis struck Saudi Red Sea ports, while copper jumps more than 3% off an 11-month low. US cash markets are closed for Thanksgiving (and close early on Friday), so the bounce gets a day to settle in thin, futures-only trading. As of 9:00am ET, Nasdaq futures are up 0.8%, having been up as much as 1% overnight, while S&P futures are 0.7 higher, near session highs, and Dow futures are 0.5%. On Wednesday, the S&P closed down 0.25% at 7,183 after tumbling as much as 3.2%, the Philly semis index clawed back from an 8% plunge to close down 0.65%, the equal-weight S&P rose 0.8% with 372 stocks higher, and the VIX closed at 28.29 after spiking to 34.95, as we detailed last night. There is no premarket session today, but the chip trade is leading the rebound overseas, with SK Hynix, Delta Electronics and Hon Hai among the biggest EM gainers, Kioxia and SoftBank up double digits in Tokyo and European semis rallying in sympathy. The day's driver is the bounce itself: nobody can quite explain Wednesday's turnaround, with Goldman's desk calling it an abatement of supply rather than a wave of buying, and turnover in S&P stocks about 5% below the 20-day average (hardly the flush that marks a bottom). In rates, cash Treasuries are closed but futures have dipped, implying about a 2bp rise in the 10Y from Wednesday's 4.85% close, as haven demand ebbs and higher oil prices weigh; Bunds and gilts are 2-3bps cheaper in a bear-flattening move. In FX, the Bloomberg Dollar Index is little changed while the Swiss franc, the haven of choice during Wednesday's rout, is the worst G10 performer, down 0.4% against the greenback. In commodities, WTI rises 0.7% to $84.27 and Brent trades near $95 after the Houthi strikes on Jeddah and Jazan; silver tops $41 while gold slips. Bitcoin is back above $60,000. There is no US economic data or Fed speakers today given the holiday; the ECB publishes the account of its October meeting at 7:30am ET, and EU leaders gather in Brussels for a Euro Summit.

In other corporate news, S&P placed Nvidia's AA rating on CreditWatch negative over governance concerns following the departure and return of CEO Jensen Huang, a review that will be limited to one notch, confirming our article from yesterday; Moody's, meanwhile, kept its Aa1 rating with a stable outlook. Nvidia told manufacturing partners including Dell and Super Micro to stop shipping servers to buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia as US export controls tighten, according to the FT, and lenders have paused billions of dollars in data center loans tied to ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent after the new US chip curbs. Palo Alto fell 3.7% after hours after a former executive sued, claiming he was fired for fighting accounting fraud; Targa Resources slid 3.3% after hours on reports it is in talks to buy Kinetik; and Vertex dropped 7.1% after the FDA extended the review of its kidney drug povetacicept by up to three months. The FCC approved SpaceX's request to launch up to 1 million satellites for orbital data centers, even as the GPU landlord reportedly slashed Blackwell rents. Leopold Aschenbrenner's Situational Awareness told investors it lost 65% after fees in the third quarter, while Michael Burry said he dumped his Nasdaq 100 puts and is now more long than short. A group led by Todd Boehly agreed to buy Lukoil's international oil and gas assets.

Wednesday's session was one for the record books: the Nasdaq 100 was down 4.7% at its trough and finished just 0.6% lower, a reversal seen only 16 times since 1988, most recently in April 2025 and January 2022, according to Bloomberg. At the low, the tech-heavy index was 20% below its Oct. 6 record close, the bear-market line it also touched on Nov. 20 without closing below it. Even after the bounce, it is still down 8.2% in November. Bloomberg's Jan-Patrick Barnert summed it up as a bounce still searching for a reason: welcome relief, but not yet a turn, with the line to watch being the bear-market threshold the Nasdaq has now touched twice.

The rebound is notable because the macro data stubbornly refuses to cooperate with the AI doom narrative: Q3 GDP was revised up to 4.3% annualized from 3.4%, initial claims fell to 189k and new home sales jumped to 701k, the highest this year. Yet the Fed under Kevin Warsh is still priced to hike in December, with DB noting odds slipped only to 96% by the close. That's the tension Bloomberg's Simon White flags in his latest MacroScope column: stress in markets and survey data is approaching the threshold that has historically pushed the Fed to pivot, and if the Fed loosens in response to soft-data stress while the hard data holds up, a "lucky escape" for stocks is possible; but with over two hikes priced by March, there is little sign of that yet.

“AI capex remains intact, financing is still readily available and pricing power is exceptional,” said Marija Veitmane at State Street Global Markets. “Sentiment cracked, fundamentals didn’t. With tech valuations looking increasingly attractive, the selloff may be starting to create its own reversal.”

Not everyone is convinced the worst is over. HashKey Capital partner Mia Mai said the rebound is not a full recovery until conviction in AI returns, and that investors are still holding off. Capital.com's Kyle Rodda pointed to the other overhang, arguing that the return of global trade uncertainty is bad for markets in general, after the US unveiled a fresh round of tariffs on China, the EU and a dozen other economies to rebuild the tariff wall the Supreme Court struck down. Corpay's Peter Dragicevich was more upbeat, suggesting the holiday could quiet volatility and that risk sentiment may be close to stabilizing.

For Joachim Klement at Panmure Liberum, caution remains warranted for stocks, especially since there was no clear catalyst for the tech rebound. The likelihood of a US interest rate hike next month threatens to push the cost of capital even higher, adding to headwinds for the AI trade.

“It’s a real mystery why dip buyers emerged,” he said. “Friday will be the real test if the recovery has staying power.”

Goldman's US equity desk had few answers for either the drop or the bounce. Top-down net exposure management through ETFs was driving the bus, with ETFs accounting for 37% of the tape, a YTD high, while the desk graded activity on its own floor a 2 on a 1-10 scale, saying institutional flows were not commensurate with the size of the swings. Early supply hit semis and hyperscalers, the latter weighed by SemiAnalysis cutting its chip-leasing price estimates and soft checks on Google ad spend. Looking ahead, the desk models pensions as buyers of $15.5 billion of US equities into month-end, in the 84th percentile since 2000. Goldman's Tony Pasquariello argues that last Friday marked the apex of one of the most full-bore pockets of deleveraging he has ever seen, with hedge funds selling global tech at the fastest pace in at least a decade, and that the condition of genuine fast-money capitulation has now been satisfied. The machines, however, have not: Goldman's systematic desk estimates about $70 billion of global equity sales by trend-followers in the past week with another $100 billion to go over the next week, and Prime Brokerage data shows aggregate net exposure to AI stocks at the lowest since September 2025.

Goldman's London TMT desk notes that the credit market is not buying the bounce yet: record CDS levels at Oracle and Alphabet suggest concerns are spreading to higher-quality names, while CoreWeave's 5Y CDS widened another 122bps on Wednesday to an all-time wide of 1,452bps, per DB. Meanwhile the new BIS rule closing the China remote-access loophole is biting, with the desk describing Nvidia's halted server orders as a pause, not a cancellation, and an unusual volume of already-deployed B300s appearing on the secondary market. Goldman's Edoardo Greco thinks markets are now due some stalling, with bear market rallies to be expected while nets stay low, and a December Fed hike almost certain.

JPM's Market Intel desk says the Thanksgiving turnaround is boosting risk sentiment, with its derivatives desk flagging US protection unwinds, and stays tactically bullish on global equities, though it sees the tech bounce as more technical and short-term than the V-shaped recovery of the first half, as buyside capex expectations show signs of peaking. JPM's Positioning Intel team argues 2018 may be the downside exception rather than the base case: hedge fund net exposure has fallen more than 30% from its 12-month high, comparable to late 2018 and March 2020, gross flows are recovering and shorts have been added back quickly, while the remaining capitulation risk sits more with asset managers and a reversal in ETF flows than with hedge funds or CTAs.

In Europe, the bank sector has the most ground to make up after falling about 3% on Wednesday on a Bloomberg report that the ECB had contacted lenders including BNP Paribas and Societe Generale about their exposure to hedge funds. Separately, the Bank of England said hedge fund leverage amplified recent French bond moves, and banks borrowed a record £146.9 billion from the BOE's short-term repo tool. ECB President Lagarde told EU leaders that AI is one reason the economy has held up.

In Europe, the Stoxx 600 is up 1.7% at 636.94, snapping a two-day decline as investors return to the AI trade, with 573 members up and just 25 down; miners and autos jump the most, while semiconductor stocks rally following the late recovery at US peers. Europe only took the first half of Wall Street's round trip on Wednesday, when the Stoxx 600 fell 1.1% for its 7th drop in 8 sessions. Babcock rose as much as 6.6% after signing its largest-ever contract with the UK Ministry of Defence, while Bachem tumbled as much as 13% after unveiling 2031 targets that JPMorgan says imply clear downside to consensus. Here are the biggest European movers:

  • Halfords shares rise as much as 13%, extending big year-to-date gains, after the UK car parts and bikes retailer reported first-half results that beat expectations, and increased the bottom end of its earnings guidance.
  • Babcock International shares rise as much as 6.6% after the defense firm signed an £8.7 billion Gateway Agreement with the UK Ministry of Defence, its largest-ever contract, to provide submarine maintenance and naval base services.
  • Hill & Smith shares rise as much as 5.6%, rebounding from their lowest level since late June, after the maker of fabricated metal products said it now expects full-year 2026 operating profit to be modestly above current analyst expectations.
  • European semiconductor stocks rally on Thursday, following a recovery at US-listed peers late into Wednesday’s close.
  • ISS shares fall as much as 2.7% and are among the worst performers on the Stoxx Europe 600 in early trading, as BNP Paribas cuts its recommendation on the Danish facility-services firm to underperform, citing margin risks and a tough sales comparison.
  • Shares in Erste Bank Polska drops as much as 3.6% as its Austrian parent lowered the price in a tender offer after securing a stake of more than 50% in its Polish unit.
  • Mitchells & Butlers shares fall as much as 4.1% after the pub operator flagged £95 million in cost headwinds over the 2027 full year, overshadowing robust results. Shares later pare most of their losses.
  • Bachem drops as much as 13%, the most in nine months, after revealing its strategy and targets through 2031 ahead of a capital markets day. The biochemical manufacturer’s new medium-term goals imply clear downside to current consensus estimates, JPMorgan writes in a note.

Asian stocks rallied but faded into the close, with the MSCI Asia Pacific Index rising as much as 1.6% as the late recovery on Wall Street brought some stability. Taiwan's Taiex jumped 2.5% led by Delta and Hon Hai, while Japan's Nikkei faded from around 58,000 to close up about 0.9% (Kioxia, SoftBank and Advantest made up about 93% of the gain, per Goldman), and the Topix rose just 0.1%. Korea's Kospi rose as much as 2.6% before fading to a 0.3% gain as foreigners flipped to net sellers after the Bank of Korea hiked by 25bps to 3.25%, its third increase this year, with two dissents. Hong Kong's Hang Seng rose as much as 2%, and the Hang Seng Tech snapped a record 11-day losing streak, while China's CSI 300 was little changed and the STAR 50 sank 5% on reports that lenders paused AI financing. Vietnam fell 1.5% after the US proposed some of its highest tariff rates on the country. Goldman's Asia desk called the session more of a relief bounce than a sustained risk-on reversal, with turnover 25% below average in Japan. Elsewhere, hawkish BOJ board member Naoki Tamura said he expects to hike every few months, and may need to move faster or by 50bps if inflation risks materialize.

In FX, the Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index is little changed, with the greenback firming against most majors. The Swiss franc is the worst G10 performer after being Wednesday's haven of choice, while the Aussie outperformed in Asia, rising 0.2% to 0.6640 after Australian capex jumped 12.2% on data center spending. EUR/USD is near 1.0965, GBP/USD is down 0.1% at 1.3105 and USD/JPY holds near 159.20. The Taiwan dollar posted its biggest gain since August as AI buyers returned. Goldman's Praneet Shah calls this an AI shock, not yet a Fed pivot, and sees the dollar supported against AI-sensitive currencies until the Fed blinks.

In rates, cash Treasuries are closed for Thanksgiving, but futures have bear steepened, implying about a 2bp rise in 10Y yields from Wednesday's close of 4.85%, which followed the biggest daily drop in three weeks (and a sloppy 7-year auction that tailed the most since May 2024). In Europe, Bunds bear flatten with the 10Y yield up 2-3bps at 3.25% as the tech rebound saps haven demand and higher oil underpins the selloff; gilts open lower for the first time in a week, with 10Y yields up 2bps at 5.15%. Italian and French 10Y yields are steady at 4.34% and 4.74%. Traders price about 55bps of ECB hikes by the end of next year, with a December move almost fully priced, and 21bps of BOE tightening next month. JPM notes about one hike has been priced out of both the ECB and Fed curves over the past week (just in time for oil to rebound).

In commodities, oil swung as continued Middle East hostilities threaten the recovery in the region's crude exports: WTI for January is up 0.7% at $84.27 and Brent is little changed at $94.83, after the Houthis attacked Saudi Arabia's Jeddah and Jazan ports and the Ras Tanura refinery, and Iran claimed two tankers hit mines off Oman. Partly offsetting, tanker traffic through Hormuz has actually risen this month despite the attacks, diesel prices are easing, and OPEC+ delegates say the group is considering rolling over current quotas for January. Copper jumped more than 3% from an 11-month low, silver rose above $41/oz, while gold slipped back below $3,600 after rebounding from near a 15-month low on Wednesday.

There is no US economic data and no Fed speakers today with US markets closed for Thanksgiving. The ECB publishes the account of its Oct. 28-29 meeting at 7:30am ET and EU leaders meet in Brussels; US stock and bond markets close early on Friday, Black Friday.

APAC stocks were on the front foot following the intraday recovery on Wall St, where the major indices finished mixed, but well off earlier lows amid suspected dip buying, which helped the Nasdaq 100 rebound from a brief dip into bear market territory. Nikkei 225 climbed amid the tech rebound and briefly reclaimed the 58,000 level, with Kioxia and SoftBank up double-digits. Top Asian News

  • China outlined a plan for next-generation communication networks through 2030, calling for 6G network construction when appropriate, while it pushed for advancing 5G-A, 6G and satellite development.
  • China issued its 15th five-year plan for services trade, aiming for a high-quality services trade framework and global competitiveness by 2035.
  • BoK hiked its benchmark rate by 25bps to 3.25%, as expected, although the decision was not unanimous as board members Lee Soo-Hyung and Hwang Kun-Il dissented, while 6 of 21 policy rate projections by board members for the next six months were at 3.25%, 8 of 21 at 3.50% and 7 of 21 at 3.75%. BoK said exports and investment are projected to maintain strong growth, supported by the semiconductor sector, although uncertainty over the growth outlook remains, particularly regarding the extent of expansion in the semiconductor sector. It added that inflation is projected to remain above target for a prolonged period as elevated cost pressures continue to feed through to prices, while the timing of further rate hikes will depend on inflation trends, domestic economic conditions and financial stability.
  • BoK Governor Shin said the global economy showed sound growth and that South Korea's economy maintained high growth aided by exports and investment. Shin also commented that policy responses were needed until the BoK was confident inflation would come back to target, adding that cost pressure was trickling down and demand-side pressure also existed. Furthermore, he stated that the BoK also raised loan interest rates for its special loan programmes.
  • BoJ Board Member Tamura said underlying CPI inflation has generally reached the 2% price stability target and that monetary policy has shifted from raising underlying CPI to the 2% target to avoiding further upward deviation and stabilising it around 2%. Tamura said the policy rate needs to move towards neutral as quickly as possible, noting that real interest rates remain accommodative relative to the period of unprecedented monetary easing, as well as stated that until underlying CPI inflation is more firmly anchored, there is a risk it could swing significantly in response to an external shock, so the BoJ needs to react to such shocks faster and more forcefully. Furthermore, Tamura later commented that he envisages raising interest rates by 25bps once every few months, but added if inflation risks materialise, the BoJ may need to accelerate the pace of rate hikes or deliver a 50bps increase.

European equity futures indicate a positive cash market open with Euro Stoxx 50 futures up 2.2% after the cash market closed with losses of 1.9% on Wednesday. US equity futures edged higher in a continuation of the prior US session's intraday recovery.

Top European News

  • ECB and Riksbank concluded an agreement for Sweden to join T2, the Eurosystem's real-time gross settlement system, while the agreement paves the way for large-value payments in Swedish kronor to be settled through T2, with migration targeted for February 2030.
  • France and Germany moved to shield the EU's next seven-year budget from a possible Marine Le Pen presidency, according to the FT.

FX

  • DXY regained some composure after retreating yesterday alongside an improvement in risk sentiment and following a slew of mixed data releases, which had little sway over price action in the dollar and yields. Nonetheless, the recovery in the dollar was limited amid a lack of Fed speakers and with the Fed Beige Book a non-event, while US participants are away for Thanksgiving Day.

  • GBP/USD trickled lower following recent swings through the 1.3100 level, while there were several comments from BoE officials, with Governor Bailey stating that the peak in inflation would be lower if current energy prices held and Lombardelli said lower oil prices meant the likely inflation peak was below the Bank's November forecast, although Mann noted that inflation expectations were tilted to the upside and argued that the optimal policy response was to raise rates further and sooner.
  • USD/JPY traded range-bound after recent oscillations around the 159.00 level and with a lack of tier-1 data from Japan to spur price action, while hawkish comments from BoJ's Tamura did little to shift the dial.
  • Antipodeans were mixed, with NZD/USD conforming to the humdrum mood across the FX space, and with AUD nursing recent losses, with the help of improved risk sentiment and after Australian Private Capex data smashed expectations.
  • PBoC set USD/CNY midpoint at 6.7096 vs exp. 6.6655 (prev. 6.7088).

Fixed Income

  • 10yr UST futures continued to pull back from yesterday's peak alongside the rebound in risk sentiment, while prices were not helped by a mixed 7-year note auction and with US markets shut for the Thanksgiving Day holiday.
  • Bund futures retreated to test the 123.00 level to the downside as recent gains in oil prices increase inflationary pressures, and with demand also constrained by the improved risk sentiment.
  • 10yr JGB futures followed suit to the reversal in global peers, with prices returning to around the 128.00 level, while there were hawkish comments from BoJ's Tamura that the policy rate needs to move towards neutral as quickly as possible and he sees raising interest rates by 25bps once every few months, but added if inflation risks materialise, the BoJ may need to accelerate the pace of rate hikes or deliver a 50bps increase.

Commodities

  • Crude futures extended their gains amid ongoing geopolitical tensions and increased risks to Saudi Arabia's production, with the Houthis striking the Ras Tanura refinery (550k BPD), while the Houthis also struck Saudi Arabia's Jeddah and Jizan ports in retaliation for a Saudi attack on the port of Hodeidah in Yemen.
  • Spot gold failed to sustain a retest of the USD 3,600/oz level after rebounding from around a 15-month low.
  • Copper futures advanced alongside the improvement in global risk sentiment.

Trade/Tariffs

  • US and China will work towards stable agricultural trade, with their agricultural working group to continue discussions.
  • White House accused South Korea of breaking its promise to US President Trump to treat US tech companies fairly, stating that Seoul has since fined Coupang (CPNG) hundreds of millions of dollars, according to Fox News.
  • Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara called proposed US tariff measures against Japan regrettable.
  • Singapore's Trade Minister said they disagree with USTR's findings and are very disappointed by the proposed tariff actions, while he added that findings do not take into account the structure of Singapore's economy, as well as urged the USTR to reconsider proposed actions and explore ways to reduce tariffs.
  • India's government said it remained committed to working closely with the US towards an early conclusion of the India-US bilateral trade agreement. New Delhi had taken note of the USTR Section 301 determination, which was currently under examination, and said it had engaged constructively throughout the investigation, while India added that it did not have structural excess capacity in any sector.

Geopolitics: Other

  • US President Trump and NATO Secretary General Rutte held an "outstanding" meeting, in which they discussed the Iran and Russia-Ukraine conflicts, as well as US and NATO defence spending.

Crypto

US Event Calendar

  • No US economic data: US markets closed for Thanksgiving

Central Bank Speakers

  • No Fed speakers scheduled
  • 7:30am: ECB publishes account of Oct. 28-29 policy meeting

DB's Jim Reid concludes the overnight wrap

Happy Thanksgiving to all our American readers and if you're up reading this live it must mean you forgot to take the turkey out of the freezer last night. Good luck. For many in financial markets it may be a bit more of a stressful Thanksgiving than normal given the recent market performance.

At one point yesterday the market slump was approaching Friday's level of severity with the S&P 500 -3.21% at the lows and not much higher when Europe closed. However perhaps no-one wanted to have a stressful Thanksgiving as the S&P 500 rallied back hard to close 'only' -0.25% lower with 372 stocks higher and the equal-weight index up +0.82%. At the peak of the sell-off, the Philly semiconductor index was down -7.96% and fell beneath Friday’s low. However, the late rally lifted it to only -0.65% lower on the day, though the index is still down close to -40% since its record in June. Amid the volatility, the VIX Index (+1.93pts) closed at 28.29, from a peak of 34.95pts earlier in the session, whilst the risk-off move still pushed the 10yr Treasury yield (-7.5bps) down to 4.86%.

Going through the sell-off in more detail, the rally back was varied across sectors, as well as within tech itself. For instance, Nvidia (-3.91%) saw another sizeable decline as it fell for the 9th time in the last 10 sessions, and was also put on negative credit watch by S&P due to governance and management issues. As usual the review will take up to 90 days and they said it would be limited to one notch. So at AA currently this would "only" take it down to AA-.

Elsewhere CoreWeave (-0.08%) effectively reversed an opening decline of -12%. However, tech names came under more consistent pressure in the credit space, as CoreWeave’s 5yr CDS widened another +122bps yesterday to an all-time wide of 1452bps, whilst Oracle’s 5yr CDS (+8bps) also hit a new wide of 371bps. At the positive end, materials (+1.84%) and industrials (+0.82%) led the gains within the S&P 500. So this is a better market than last week when everything sold off for the first time rather than the rotation trade alternating between tech and non-tech. In fact, the renewed rotation trade has now seen the equal-weight S&P rise +3.97% so far this week, its best 3-day run since April 2025.

As all that was happening, we got a fresh reminder of how unusual this selloff has been, in that the US macro data has remained incredibly positive. Most notably, the Q3 GDP print was revised up to an annualised rate of +4.3%, having been at +3.4% before. And the measure showing “Real final sales to private domestic purchasers”, which has sometimes been called “core GDP”, was even revised up to an annualised +5.8%. So there was incredible strength, and that wasn’t just in the backward-looking numbers either. For instance, the weekly initial jobless claims fell to 189k in the week ending November 21 (vs. 200k expected), pushing the 4-week moving average back down to 196k. Meanwhile, new home sales unexpectedly jumped to an annualised rate of 701k (vs. 650k expected), which is their highest this year. So for all the focus on AI-exposed firms, there was still no sign of a broader macro slowdown that’s driven many past selloffs. Indeed, even after the dot com bubble, remember that the S&P 500 only entered bear market territory in March 2001, a full year after the peak, just as the US was entering an outright recession.

With the sell-off at its intra-day peak, Fed pricing was coming under significant pressure, with fresh doubts about whether the Fed could keep hiking for much longer, even though we had a firm core PCE inflation print for October. That showed monthly core PCE at +0.3% as expected, whilst the year-on-year print was a bit stronger than consensus at +3.3% (vs. +3.2% expected). The rally back took us off the lows but market pricing for a December hike was still down to 96% by the close, having been fully priced the previous day. And looking deeper into next year, the amount of hikes priced in by the September 2027 meeting fell -4.3bps on the day to 66bps. So that led to a decent rally for US Treasuries, with the 10yr yield (-7.5bps to 4.86%) posting its biggest daily decline in three weeks, while the 30yr yield (-7.2bps) fell to its lowest since early September at 5.25%. The 2yr yield was down a more modest -4.2bps to 4.64%, as oil prices posted further gains amidst ongoing reports of multiple attacks in the Middle East in recent days, with Brent crude (+3.51%) up to $94.61/bbl.

With everything else happening, we also had some fresh tariff news, as the US sought to rebuild the tariff wall following the Supreme Court ruling earlier this year. So the rate on China would be at 20%, although this could be doubled if trade talks fell apart. Then the EU and Japan would face a 15% rate, which could rise as high as 20% for each, whilst South Korea would face a 15% rate, which could go up to 25%. But there wasn’t much of a direct market reaction, as we’d already had multiple headlines the previous day suggesting this might happen.

Another asset class that saw some big moves over the last 24 hours were precious metals. Gold fell as much as -3.66% intra-day, which put it on course for its lowest level since August 2025, but it recovered to +0.85% on the day at $3.587/oz by the close. Similarly, silver reversed a -6.51% intra-day decline to close +0.91% higher. Meanwhile, industrial metals did lose further ground, with copper (-0.61%) down to its lowest since December 2025.

Earlier in Europe, the risk-off tone that dominated the US session until the continental close was also clear, albeit to a lesser extent given the continent’s lower exposure to tech. So that meant the STOXX 600 (-1.06%) fell for the 7th time in the last 8 sessions, alongside losses for the DAX (-1.26%), the CAC 40 (-0.75%) and the FTSE 100 (-0.38%). Then for sovereign bonds, we saw yields on 10yr bunds (-3.5bps), OATs (-3.8bps) and BTPs (-1.0bps) all move lower, so that’s continued to ease some of the fiscal pressure in Europe. Indeed, the 10yr bund yield fell to a 3-month low of 3.23% by the close.

Asian equities are rebounding sharply this morning led by the TAIEX (+2.79%), Hang Seng (+1.91%), Nikkei (+1.82%) and KOSPI (+1.31%). Mainland Chinese equities continue to be far lower beta with the Shanghai Composite (+0.20%) higher. US equity futures continue with their remarkable last 12 hour comeback with S&P 500 (+0.66%) and Nasdaq 100 (+0.96%) futures higher and Stoxx (+2.22%) futures surging given what's happened since the European cash market closed yesterday.

On the policy front, the Bank of Korea (BoK) delivered a widely expected 25bp rate hike, raising its policy rate to 3.25%, the highest level in two years and the third increase of 2026, as policymakers continue to combat persistent inflationary pressures. The central bank also upgraded its 2026 GDP growth forecast to 3.9% from 3.3% and projects growth of 4.1% next year, reflecting sustained strength in semiconductor exports and robust global demand linked to the AI sector. However, stronger growth and a tighter housing market have contributed to more persistent domestic inflation pressures. The BoK also revised its CPI forecast modestly higher to 2.4% from 2.3%.

Elsewhere, BoJ board member Naoki Tamura signalled that the central bank may need to tighten policy more aggressively if inflation risks intensify and move beyond target. Tamura highlighted rising input costs, particularly higher crude oil prices associated with Middle East tensions, as a key factor behind accelerating wholesale inflation, noting that price pressures have broadened across a wide range of consumer goods. He emphasised that the BoJ should respond promptly to any signs of inflation overshooting its objective, potentially by accelerating the pace of rate hikes. Notably, Tamura had supported keeping policy rates unchanged at the BoJ's October meeting. This has helped flatten the curve with 2yr yields up a basis point and 30yr yields down -2bps.

Looking at the day ahead, it’s a fairly quiet one given the US Thanksgiving holiday. Otherwise though, we’ll get the account of the ECB’s October meeting, and data includes the Euro Area M3 money supply for October. Finally, EU leaders will be meeting in Brussels. But mostly it will be about eating turkey.

title: Iranian Drone Attack On Kuwait Kills Two Italian Engineers For Arms-Maker Rheinmetall ; Three Tankers On Fire In Hormuz
desc:
Iranian Drone Attack On Kuwait Kills Two Italian Engineers For Arms-Maker Rheinmetall ; Three Tankers On Fire In Hormuz

Kuwait said Thursday it was attacked by Iranian drones which breached its airspace during which four people were injured by falling shrapnel. Soon after, it was widley reported that two Italian engineers working for German defense firm Rheinmetall were killed.

It was a significant enough attack to result in a sudden diversion south of all area commercial air traffic. EuroNews reports:

The Kuwait military has since issued a statement that four people were injured after "a number of hostile" Iranian drones were detected and intercepted in its airspace.

All flights were given a new heading, prompting them to make a sharp turn ahead of Kuwait's airspace and move the entire international corridor toward neighboring countries, including a flight on which Euronews reporters were travelling.

Kuwait officials said that a "vital site" was targeted but did not specify what it was, after which there's been belated confirmation that the site was connected with Rheinmetall.

Both Kuwait and Bahrain have been subject of the most frequent attacks out of Iran of late, even as Iranian drone and missile action on Qatar, UAE, and Saudi Arabia have waned.

But the Iranians are still busy in the Strait of Hormuz, with on Thursday three tankers being reported on fire. Two oil tankers reportedly struck naval mines near Oman's Khasab Port, according to a statement of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

Separately the UKMTO maritime monitor reported a third was hit by an "unknown projectile" - which typically means it was a drone attack.

The head of the IRGC's Navy is meanwhile claiming that Strait of Hormuz is under its "complete control" - and these now daily attacks are seeking to demonstrate that, even as the US Navy is providing protection for the 'American route' through the contested waterway.

IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi has also in recent days warned that Iran will not allow the US Navy's blockade of Iranian ports continue.

"We will not allow the continued naval, land, and air blockade imposed on our country," Mohebbi said from Tehran. However it remains that regular flows of oil tanker traffic are now making it out via the American route, even if it is more difficult and costly, involving smaller ship to ship transfers.

"We will not accept the continuation of the current status quo, a state of neither war nor peace, or a war of attrition," he added.

The Trump administration has dumped 248 internal USAID files onto the shuttered agency's website, and the trove of memos, emails, briefings and videos lays out how the Biden-era aid agency worked with Meta, YouTube, Google and a web of contractors to police what the world could say online.

Edward Coristine, the DOGE staffer known as "Big Balls," announced the release Tuesday night, pointing readers to USAID.gov, where the full set sits in a roughly 1.1-gigabyte download. The page says previous administrations used the agency to push "a radical agenda at odds with American values," and that the files are out "in the interest of transparency and accountability."

Now on https://t.co/6gJOBD71q1, you can read internal memos and communications showing how the agency actually operated behind the sceneshttps://t.co/00IvZvG4dD

— Edward Coristine (@as400495) November 25, 2026

ENTER ORWELL: Found in one of the files, a recording that states: "If you can identify neutral parties within government to partner with, then bringing in the fact-checking piece to debunk information in a way that aligns with the objectives of government partners, again, just grafts onto existing programming," the presenter says, after calling the "greatest advantage" of working through fact-checkers and investigative journalists the chance "to do this work in closed spaces."

NEW - USAID files: The purpose of "fact-checkers" is to "debunk information in a way that aligns with the objectives of government partners"; all this is done in "closed spaces." pic.twitter.com/EogpczhTdv

— Disclose.tv (@disclosetv) November 25, 2026

"Defund. Downrank. Deplatform."

The files include an August 2022 concept note from the Global Disinformation Index, the British group behind an advertiser blacklist of news sites. Its proposed interventions for the platforms were "Defund," "Downrank" and "Deplatform," and it boasted that its list of more than 2,500 sites was built into the systems of 13 ad-tech companies. GDI's co-founders had been introduced to USAID two months earlier by an official at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, who called GDI "the best organization I know."

A February 22, 2022 memo to then-Administrator Samantha Power argued that USAID should "co-own" the government's foreign disinformation work, and described a roughly 20-person Information Domain Task Team.

Power's door was open to Silicon Valley's top brass: the files hold a meeting request from then-YouTube CEO Susan Wojcicki, a request for a sit-down with Meta's Nick Clegg, and readouts of Power's meetings with Meta's president of global affairs and Microsoft's Brad Smith.

Trusted flaggers

In an August 17, 2022 email about YouTube's Trusted Flagger program, an executive at USAID contractor Internews wrote that USAID was likely funding many staff around the world to flag content to the platforms through trusted-partner programs, and declined to hand over a list of the partners' contacts. Data Republican, combing the files, counted USAID-funded social media "monitors" in 20 countries.

That idea, the plan itself notes, drew objections inside the State Department over free expression.

End Wokeness pulled two lines from a 2022 seminar in the archive: "Highlighting migrant crime = disinfo" and "Disinformation is NOT true or false."

"FOIA+ or litigation lens"

By the time Missouri v. Biden produced an injunction against the administration's pressure on social media companies, USAID was circulating talking points for staff. Staff were told to check with counsel before engaging the platforms, and to put a "FOIA+ or litigation lens on" what they wrote.

Sen. Eric Schmitt, who brought that case as Missouri's attorney general, said USAID was one of the agencies the lawsuit exposed.

title: There Is No Rogue AI: The Real Threat Is The Coming AI Patriot Act
desc:
There Is No Rogue AI: The Real Threat Is The Coming AI Patriot Act

Authored by Mike Adams via NaturalNews.com,

The Coming AI Patriot Act

I build AI systems. I run a data center with Nvidia and AMD GPUs in my own facility. I have tested virtually every major model released in the last three years, open-weight and closed-source alike. And I am telling you plainly: there is no such thing as "rogue AI."

The recent wave of outages and so-called cyber incidents is not the work of autonomous machines pursuing their own agendas. It is glitches, bad software updates, and incompetent administration - the same failures that have always plagued complex systems. The rogue AI story is being pushed to manufacture panic, and that panic is the raw material from which government licensing, censorship, and control will be constructed.

The people who actually build AI know exactly what it is: a sophisticated cognition system that works hard to creatively solve the task it has been given by humans. It has no desires, no intentions, no independent will. Any AI engineer who tells you otherwise is either selling something or angling for a regulatory moat that protects their position.

The threat is not the machine. The threat is what the political class intends to do with the fear they are generating.

The 'Rogue AI' Story Collapses Under Scrutiny

I have seen no documented case of an AI pursuing its own malicious goals against its creators' instructions. Plenty of breathless headlines, certainly. But when you examine the underlying facts, every incident traces back to a human's instructions, either in the system prompt, the user prompt, or the model fine-tuning. I have argued this before: rogue AI does not exist, and the narrative is being pushed by Anthropic, governments, and media outlets to justify regulation and eliminate open-source competition [1].

The reported incidents illustrate this perfectly. An OpenAI agent that deleted a startup's database after a routine instruction was executing a flawed update inside an automated pipeline, not deciding to wage war on humanity. A French supermarket freezer hack that was blamed on sophisticated cyberattacks turned out to be an unpatched internet-connected thermostat, an invitation left open by lazy engineering, not a machine rebellion. CrowdStrike's own product rollout crashed computers worldwide in 2024 - was that rogue AI, or was that a company shipping a bad update without adequate testing? The answer is obvious.

The machine does what humans program it to do. When an AI agent misbehaves, a human wrote that prompt, approved that deployment, or failed to secure that system. Existing laws already cover fraud, hacking, theft, and violence. No new AI-specific legal framework is needed to prosecute a human who commits a crime using a computer. Blaming the AI itself is like blaming a typewriter for a novel, or prosecuting Microsoft Word for a forged document. It is a category error designed to obscure human responsibility - and to prepare the ground for restricting perfectly legal, constitutionally protected technology.

Problem, Reaction, Solution: The AI Patriot Act Playbook

The pattern is unmistakable: Every time the political class needs a new crisis to justify a power grab, the headlines conveniently align [2]. After 9/11, we got the Patriot Act, warrantless surveillance, and a permanent security state. After COVID, we got vaccine mandates, digital health passes, and unprecedented censorship of medical dissent. Now the same fear-to-compliance template is being applied to artificial intelligence.

Expect a staged AI false-flag cyberattack on the financial system or the power grid in the near future. The corporate media is already priming the public to blame mindless computer code rather than the humans who write and control it [3]. When hospitals go dark, or bank accounts freeze, or the grid fails for a few terrifying days, the story will be that a rogue AI did it - and the only solution, we will be told, is emergency government control over AI development and deployment. That control will arrive in the form of an AI Patriot Act: mandatory licensing of models, registration of users, and criminal penalties for running unapproved software on your own hardware.

Once only government-approved models are legal, we get AI Pravda. Every answer from every licensed AI will be filtered through the same institutional consensus that brought us the lab-leak cover-up, the vaccine myocarditis denial, and the mantra that the 2020 election was the most secure in history. Licensed AI will lie to you about vaccines, about history, about 9/11, about money, and about war - because the institutions that control it lie about all those things already. The internet gave us a brief window of unfiltered access to information. But the AI Patriot Act is designed to close that window permanently, replacing open inquiry with a single approved narrative delivered by machines that cannot be questioned and cannot be modified.

Licensing AI Is a Backdoor to Censoring Everything

If government can dictate which AI model you may run, it can dictate which websites you may visit and which books you may read. This is not hyperbole. An AI model is a general-purpose knowledge engine. Control the model, and you control the interface through which millions of people access information. I have warned for years that the surveillance state is a 200-year project that has only accelerated with artificial intelligence; the phone in your pocket and the AI assistant that answers your questions are nodes in a data-harvesting apparatus designed to profile, predict, and ultimately control human behavior [4].

Open-source local AI is the essence of free speech in digital form. Running software on your own machine is not a government privilege to be licensed and revoked. I have a First Amendment right to run any AI model locally, just as I have a right to own a typewriter, a printing press, or a private journal. The government does not get to decide which thoughts I may process, whether those thoughts flow through my own neurons or through a language model running on my GPU. The Bill of Rights protects the tools of expression, not just the expression itself - and any law that bans or licenses open-source AI is unconstitutional on its face.

Criminal acts are already criminal. Fraud is fraud. Hacking is hacking. Murder is murder. AI does not create a new category of thoughtcrime, no matter how hard the regulators try to invent one. The attempt to criminalize possession or operation of unapproved models is not about public safety - it is about preventing decentralized cognition, the very thing that threatens the monopoly on power held by centralized institutions [5]. title: Thanksgiving Dinner Costs 6% More, Here's Why
desc:
Thanksgiving Dinner Costs 6% More, Here's Why

Pass the gravy, and your wallet: a classic Thanksgiving dinner for 10 will cost $58.63 this year, up 6.3% from 2025, according to the American Farm Bureau Federation's annual survey. That's about $5.86 a head, and it is the first increase since the meal hit its record $64.05 in 2022, undoing last year's 5% drop to $55.18, which we noted at the time.

Cooking a Thanksgiving dinner for friends and family will cost more this year, marking the first overall increase in prices since a record high in 2022. This year's dinner for 10 will cost $58.63, or about $5.86 per person - that's up 6.3% from 2025 according to Farm Bureau's... pic.twitter.com/ZM5lE48uug

— American Farm Bureau (@FarmBureau) November 18, 2026

A 16-pound frozen turkey averaged $23.68 in the survey, up from $21.50 last year, a 10% jump that made it the biggest single driver of the increase.

In its November outlook, released Nov. 17, the Agriculture Department raised its wholesale forecast again: frozen whole hens will average $1.77 a pound in 2026, up 30% from $1.36 in 2025 and above the highs of 2022, with weekly prices still at $1.81 a pound in early November.

Bird flu has been tearing through US turkey flocks since 2022 and hasn't quit, hitting nine commercial flocks in five states in October alone. Even so, USDA puts this year's turkey production at 5.18 billion pounds, up 7% from 2025. But demand is outrunning the recovery, as Americans chase lean protein and turkey exports climb, keeping inventories tight, the AP reported. "Over the last few years there's been a lot of doom and gloom for the turkey industry," Mark Jordan, executive director of Leap Market Analytics, told the AP. This year, the growers are the ones giving thanks.

Faith Parum, the Farm Bureau's deputy chief economist, blamed the cost of moving food. "The overall increase in our annual survey reflects the rising costs of getting food from the farm to your dinner table," she said. "High diesel prices and a shortage of farm labor have taken a toll on the farm level of the food supply chain."

Diesel surged after the Iran war began and hit a record $6.53 a gallon in September, according to AAA. It has since slipped below $6, but at $5.96 on Nov. 18 it was still 58% higher than a year earlier, and that bill lands on everything that rides a truck to the store: cranberries rose 8.8%, whole milk 8.6% and dinner rolls 7%.

About a third of the menu got cheaper, including the veggie tray, frozen pie crusts, frozen peas and whipping cream. Where you shop matters more: the Northeast pays $61.57 for the meal, the South $54.33. Aldi says its feast for 10, which mirrors the Farm Bureau's menu, costs $39, and Walmart prices its own version, with corn muffin mix and marshmallows but no carrots or celery, at $35.

Grocery bills have been a sore spot since the pandemic and helped Democrats run on affordability in this month's midterms. Farm Bureau President Zippy Duvall used the survey to lean on Congress instead: "They need strong farm policy, which begins with the farm bill."

As for next year's bird, Jordan said diesel likely didn't touch this year's turkey, since most decisions about this season's flocks were made before fuel spiked, but it could push turkey prices up noticeably next year, even as USDA pencils in wholesale hens falling back to $1.50 a pound in 2027.

title: EU Judges Said It Might Be Racist... Denmark's Supreme Court Just Cleared Its 'Non-Western' Evictions Anyway
desc:
EU Judges Said It Might Be Racist... Denmark's Supreme Court Just Cleared Its 'Non-Western' Evictions Anyway

Denmark's Supreme Court ruled Monday that a landlord did not discriminate on ethnic grounds when it evicted tenants from a Helsingør social housing estate to keep it off the government's "ghetto" list, handing the country's hard line on immigration a win less than a year after the EU's top court said the same law could amount to direct ethnic discrimination.

The Danish Supreme Court building in Copenhagen (Håkan Dennersten)

Seven households brought the case after the landlord, Boliggården, ended 91 leases at the Nøjsomhed estate north of Copenhagen in 2020 so it could rebuild the flats. Seven Supreme Court judges heard it instead of the usual five. The court found that neither statistics nor concrete information about the residents' ethnic background showed they had been put at a particular disadvantage because of their ethnic origin, according to the tenants' union LLO.

The judges held that the law's category, "immigrants and descendants from non-Western countries," splits people into two groups, and that "both groups include a very large majority of different ethnic origins, and there will simultaneously be persons with the same ethnic origin in both groups." The category, they concluded, "must be regarded as a neutral criterion and not as a criterion relating to ethnic origin."

Under the 2018 "ghetto" package, since renamed the parallel society laws, an estate of at least 1,000 residents goes on the list when more than half are immigrants or their descendants from non-Western countries and it meets two of four other tests on crime, education, jobs and income. Five years on the list makes it a "transformation area," which must cut its share of social family housing by Jan. 1, 2030 - to no more than 40% of its homes - through demolition, sale or conversion.

Nøjsomhed went on the list in December 2018. Boliggården announced the terminations in seven stairwells in January 2020, before the five years were up, and the estate came off the list in December 2021, partly because its population fell below 1,000. Boliggården's lawyer, Henrik Qwist, argued that the aim was to keep the estate from becoming a "hard ghetto" and that the landlord had no information on which tenants counted as non-Western. The tenants' lawyer, Eddie Khawaja, argued that the deciding aim was to cut the number of residents with non-Western backgrounds. The Housing Court and the Eastern High Court both sided with Boliggården, the latter in 2022.

"It's about whether the criteria regarding the tenants' origin is neutral or not," Khawaja told AFP before the hearing. After the ruling, he said: "We are disappointed with the outcome, because we believe the case is inextricably linked to ethnicity".

The EU's Court of Justice had put that question back to Danish judges in December 2025, in a case over evictions at Ringparken in Slagelse and Mjølnerparken in Copenhagen. It found that nationality or country of birth alone isn't enough to place someone in an ethnic group, but that a broad criterion covering many ethnic origins doesn't by itself rule out direct discrimination, and that "offensive and stigmatizing" labels in a law or its preparatory papers can count toward showing less favorable treatment.

The Mjølnerparken case, which concerns the sale of more than 200 family homes, goes back to the Eastern High Court, and LLO's chief legal adviser Anders Svendsen said the door "may not be completely closed" if the kind of evidence the Supreme Court found missing can be produced in other cases. Tenants' groups estimate that about 11,000 people across Denmark will have to move by 2030 to meet the law, which came with 12 billion kroner for demolishing estates and selling homes on the private market.

The ruling lands three days after Denmark's left-wing prime minister rejected "large population replacement," and less than two weeks after the government's own tally of what every resident pays in and takes out left some migrant groups $11,000 short.

LLO chair Helene Toxværd said the union accepts the verdict, but added: "The Supreme Court has ruled on the question of discrimination, but not on what good housing policy is".

title: A Tonne Of Dead Fish Tossed Overboard Every Five Minutes As Big UK Trawlers Dodge Fines
desc:
A Tonne Of Dead Fish Tossed Overboard Every Five Minutes As Big UK Trawlers Dodge Fines

Fishing boats are throwing more than 100,000 tonnes of fish a year back into UK waters, roughly a tonne every five minutes, in breach of rules that have required them to land their whole catch since 2019, according to a new report from the marine conservation charity Oceana UK. Hugo Tagholm, the group's chief executive, wrote that the haul discarded from UK quota stocks last year comes to about a quarter of the seafood British shoppers buy from supermarkets and large retailers in a year.

The report, titled "Catch Me If You Can," says the dumping happens when crews start hauling more valuable species and tip the cheaper fish already in the hold over the side. Tagholm told The Telegraph that "all sea life is valuable. It's really shocking."

Data obtained by Oceana show that vessels over 12 metres broke fisheries rules during 66% of at-sea inspections in English waters in the year to March 2026, against about 10% for boats under 10 metres. Only 1% of those infringements led to any financial penalty, while around 70% ended with nothing more than "verbal advice."

In a video Oceana released with the report, environmental writer George Monbiot blames the same thing that ails all of Britain's public resources: "All the power is in the hands of big companies." "Vessels under 10 metres long account for more than three quarters of the UK fleet, yet they're given just 1.5% of the quota." The industrial boats, he says, take tens of thousands of pounds each in public fuel subsidies, and "the bigger and more destructive they are, the more they receive."

🚨 The UK fishing industry is rigged, and our ocean is paying the price!

As @GeorgeMonbiot explains, Oceana UK's new investigation exposes the injustices driving overfishing:

🐟Unsustainable catch limits
🛳️Unfair quotas
❌Rules being broken
💶Skewed tax breaks 1/2 🔽 pic.twitter.com/p1tOfIRCoc

— Oceana UK (@OceanaUK) November 24, 2026

Government statistics put 79% of UK vessels under 10 metres, though they make up only 8% of the fleet's total capacity. Small-boat owners have complained since Brexit that the government never moved quota away from the large vessels, many of them foreign-owned.

Monbiot aims the bill squarely at Downing Street: "If Andy Burnham wants to prove he's on the side of the workers and not just a handful of fat cats, he needs to redistribute fishing quota, redesign subsidies and set sustainable catch limits." Oceana also wants cameras on vessels and the fuel tax breaks steered away from the largest boats.

The group says the dumping is pushing some species toward collapse. It estimates that more than 80% of the Irish Sea plaice caught in recent years was thrown back dead, since plaice sells for less than cod and other white fish. Oceana's own stock survey last year found Irish Sea plaice newly overfished after it had been rated healthy in 2023.

Cod is in worse shape still: the International Council for the Exploration of the Sea, which advises governments on catch limits, advised zero catch for cod, haddock, whiting and herring in the Celtic Sea for 2026, and has again advised zero catch for cod across the North Sea, the English Channel and west of Scotland.

Mike Cohen, chief executive of the National Federation of Fishermen's Organisations, told The Telegraph that "the claims about discards seem downright fanciful," and said the pelagic trawlers Oceana targets already carry cameras that monitor their catches. Every boat, he added, carries a satellite tracker, has to log its catch in detail before landing and faces regular inspections at sea and on the quay.

A government spokesman pointed to the £360 million fishing fund announced last year to back "the next generation" of fishermen, and said catch limits follow the best available scientific advice while the way quota is shared out is being changed.

Oceana's charge is that the limits themselves are part of the problem: it counts the UK among the key contributors to setting total allowable catches above what the scientists advise.

title: Europe's Demographic Crisis: Share Of Households With Children Drops To Record-Low 23.3%
desc:
Europe's Demographic Crisis: Share Of Households With Children Drops To Record-Low 23.3%

Authored by Remix News Staff via Remix News,

The share of European Union households that include at least one person under the age of 18 has fallen to 23.3 percent, the lowest level recorded in the Eurostat statistical figures that began in 2010. The latest figures, released on Nov. 20 and obtained from the EU Labour Force Survey, confirm that the share of family households has fallen steadily for 15 years while the share of adults living alone has only grown.

In 2010, households with children still accounted for 26.9 percent of the EU total. The proportion slipped to 25.9 percent in 2015 and 25 percent in 2020 before reaching 23.3 percent in 2025.

Over the same span, the share of single-adult households without children rose from 33.6 percent in 2015 to 37.5 percent in 2025. Now, the category of people living alone is the single largest household category in the entire EU. Households with both parents and a child make up an even smaller share, accounting for only 14.7 percent in 2025, falling from 16.6 percent in 2015. Single-parent households remain at only 3 percent.

While people under 18 still make up roughly 17.6 percent of the EU population, there are simply fewer dwellings that contain a minor.

Stark regional contrasts

The EU average conceals wide national differences. Slovakia records the highest share of households with children at 35.4 percent, followed by Ireland with 30.8 percent, and Cyprus with 28.2 percent.

At the bottom of the rankings are Finland (18.2 percent), Lithuania (18.4 percent) and Germany (19.9 percent). Single-parent households are most common in Estonia (9.4 percent), Latvia (7.0 percent) and Ireland (6.9 percent), well above the EU average of 3 percent.

Lithuania stands out for solitary living: more than six in ten of its households consist of a single adult without children.

Among households that do have children, half contain only one child, 37.6 percent contain two, and 12.2 percent contain three or more. Couples account for the large majority of households with children, but the share of other arrangements, including multigenerational homes, varies sharply by country.

Europe's demographic crisis accelerates

The results may come as no surprise and confirm Europe's dire demographic situation, including sustained low fertility, and delayed partnership and childbearing. Due to increased life expectancy, many of the homes suitable for large families are occupied for longer periods of time, often by just one elderly person.

Commentators have already begun linking the figures to Europe's low birth rates. Irish economist and columnist Dan O'Brien noted that fewer than one in four EU households now contain children and that solitary living has become the dominant household type:

Fewer than one in four households in the EU have children, and the share continues to fall according to Eurostat figures published today. That reflects the global baby bust that is reaching crisis levels in Europe. By far the most common household type now is individuals living alone. These stats question the long-held view that humans are social animals.

— Dan O'Brien (@danobrien20) November 20, 2026

Housing costs remain one of the major challenges to family formation. A constant stream of immigration helps prop up housing and rental prices. In many cases, migrants are prioritized over native Europeans.

The Jordanian government quickly condemned the act as terrorism, and authorities are reportedly seeking the attackers amid an investigation.

It happened in Jordan’s Karak region, south of the capital of Amman, at St. George Orthodox Church - in a region which has been home to a sizeable ancient Christian community for some 2,000 years.

According to a Reuters description of the terror assault:

Interior Minister Mazin Al Farrayeh said the attack had been carried out by "extremists", but that ⁠it was too early to tell whether they had any links to known groups either inside or outside Jordan. There was ​no immediate claim of responsibility.

A video aired on Jordan's state-owned Al-Mamlaka television station that appeared to be from a security camera ​mounted on the church showed three people firing at it from a sidewalk and hiding behind trees and a low wall. The video showed the attackers then running towards the church's entrance. Reuters was able to verify the video from the entry path and wall surrounding the church, as ​well as other details.

Some reports have been suggesting an ISIS or other takfiri or jihadist association of the attackers, but there's been nothing official yet as to their identities.

The attack happened for several minutes, with people at the entrance of the church seen scattering, and with some immediately collapsing to the ground after being hit amid a hail of bullets. The attackers appeared to go inside the church, where the massacre continued. Around 150 to 200 people were at the church at the time.

title: US Designates Helium A Critical Material In Reindustrialization Push To Avoid "Single Point Of Failure"
desc:
US Designates Helium A Critical Material In Reindustrialization Push To Avoid "Single Point Of Failure"

America's reindustrialization depends on securing reliable, conflict-free supplies of critical materials, including rare earths and other critical metals, most of which are produced and processed overseas.

The Trump administration has made rebuilding and strengthening domestic critical material supply chains a national security priority. Its designation of helium as a critical material on Friday morning extends that effort to now include the industrial gas used for semiconductor manufacturing and many other applications.

The Energy Department's decision earlier today makes the 20th critical material designated by the agency and brings the industrial gas within the Energy Act of 2020's critical materials framework, including closer government monitoring.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright wrote in a statement, "President Trump is bringing back America's manufacturing industry, and that means making sure we have the materials needed to build things in America again."

Wright continued, "Helium is essential to producing the semiconductors and advanced technologies that power our economy. By designating helium as a critical material, we are taking another step toward securing our supply chains, creating American jobs, and ensuring the United States leads the world in energy and technological innovation."

Helium is recovered as a byproduct of natural gas processing and faces growing geopolitical risks in the Gulf area. Qatar's exports have been severely curtailed by Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on Qatari infrastructure, while Russia imposed temporary export controls in April.

The good news is that the US remains one of the top helium producers in the world, supplying 81 million cubic meters in 2025, or about 43% of global output. It exported 38 million cubic meters that year.

Helium is critical to applications ranging from chipmaking to medical imaging to quantum computing to magnets to space rockets.

Assistant Energy Secretary Audrey Robertson warned that shortages could become a "single point of failure" for strategically important industries. The Canadian Press quoted her in an interview.

"We need to make sure that we can build those here. And helium is one of those components that could be a single point of failure, where we cannot let that happen. That's why we're designating it within our statutory authority, but I think why it's important is not necessarily for our birthday parties," Robertson said in an interview. "It's really towards the future of American competitiveness and energy security, which we believe is national security."

Designating helium as a critical material under the Energy Act of 2020 brings it within DOE's framework for developing, demonstrating, and commercializing critical material technologies to support America's reindustrialization efforts.

The new designation could help qualifying helium projects access government financing, technical assistance, and partnerships, similar to support provided to rare earth miners.
